cards.q: What is IEEE 802.1Q?
cards.a: IEEE 802.1Q is the IEEE standard that defines VLAN tagging and VLAN-aware Ethernet bridging. It allows multiple VLANs to share the same physical Ethernet link by carrying a VLAN Identifier (VID) inside an Ethernet frame.

cards.q: What is the size of the 802.1Q VLAN tag and where is it inserted?
cards.a: The 802.1Q VLAN tag is 4 bytes, inserted into the Ethernet frame between the Source MAC address and the EtherType/Length field.

cards.q: What are the fields of the 802.1Q tag?
cards.a: The tag contains a 16-bit TPID and a 16-bit TCI. The TCI contains a 3-bit PCP, a 1-bit DEI, and a 12-bit VID.

cards.q: What is the TPID and its common value for an IEEE 802.1Q VLAN tag?
cards.a: TPID (Tag Protocol Identifier) is 16 bits and identifies the following field as an IEEE VLAN tag. For the common IEEE 802.1Q VLAN tag, TPID = 0x8100.

cards.q: Is the TPID the same as the VLAN ID?
cards.a: No. The TPID identifies the VLAN-tagging protocol (commonly 0x8100), while the VID identifies the VLAN.

cards.q: What is the PCP field?
cards.a: PCP (Priority Code Point) is a 3-bit field providing 8 priority values (0-7). It is used for Layer 2 traffic prioritization and is commonly associated with 802.1p priority / Class of Service (CoS).

cards.q: What is the DEI field?
cards.a: DEI (Drop Eligible Indicator) is a 1-bit field. DEI = 0 indicates not marked drop-eligible; DEI = 1 indicates marked drop-eligible during congestion.

cards.q: What is the VID and what are the valid and reserved values?
cards.a: VID (VLAN Identifier) is 12 bits and can represent 0-4095. Normal VLAN IDs are 1-4094; VLAN 0 is reserved for priority-tagged frames and VLAN 4095 is reserved.

cards.q: How many usable VLANs does a 12-bit VID provide?
cards.a: A 12-bit VID provides 4096 possible values but only 4094 usable VLAN IDs (1-4094). Do not answer 4095.

cards.q: What are the maximum frame sizes for untagged and 802.1Q-tagged Ethernet frames?
cards.a: A standard Ethernet frame with a 1500-byte Layer 3 payload has a maximum size of 1518 bytes. Adding an 802.1Q tag (+4 bytes) makes the tagged frame up to 1522 bytes.

cards.q: Does adding a 4-byte 802.1Q tag change the IP MTU to 1522?
cards.a: No. This does not mean the IP MTU automatically becomes 1522 bytes. A common configuration still uses an IP MTU of 1500 bytes while the Layer 2 frame carrying that packet can be 1522 bytes.

cards.q: How is the native VLAN handled on an 802.1Q trunk?
cards.a: The native VLAN is normally transmitted untagged on an 802.1Q trunk. Normal VLAN traffic is tagged, while native VLAN traffic is normally untagged, though Cisco can tag it with 'vlan dot1q tag native' where supported.

cards.q: Is '802.1Q means every frame is tagged' an absolute rule?
cards.a: No. It is too absolute; the normal native-VLAN behavior is the important exception, where native VLAN frames are normally untagged.

cards.q: Where is 802.1Q used?
cards.a: On switch-to-switch trunks, router-on-a-stick subinterfaces (via 'encapsulation dot1Q <vlan>'), and on firewalls, hypervisors, servers, and network appliances to support multiple logical VLAN interfaces over one physical Ethernet interface.

cards.q: How does a switch add and remove VLAN tags?
cards.a: The tag is not necessarily present for the entire path. A switch can add or remove the VLAN tag according to port and VLAN behavior; for ordinary access ports, endpoint traffic is normally untagged and the trunk adds the 802.1Q VLAN identification when forwarding across a trunk.

cards.q: How does 802.1Q differ from ISL?
cards.a: 802.1Q is an IEEE standard using a 4-byte tag inside the frame with a native VLAN concept; ISL is Cisco proprietary, uses external encapsulation with the entire frame encapsulated, and has no native VLAN concept. ISL is legacy and obsolete on modern platforms.

cards.q: What does modern Cisco trunking use, 802.1Q or ISL?
cards.a: Modern Cisco trunking uses 802.1Q. ISL is legacy Cisco technology.

cards.q: How does 802.1Q relate to QoS?
cards.a: The 802.1Q TCI contains the 3-bit PCP field, which provides Layer 2 priority information that Cisco commonly calls CoS. PCP can be used to classify traffic and map it to internal QoS queues.

cards.q: Are PCP and DSCP the same?
cards.a: No. PCP is a Layer 2 priority field within the 802.1Q tag, while DSCP is a Layer 3 IP QoS marking. They are different fields at different layers.

cards.q: What is the encapsulation command on older Cisco platforms that support configurable trunk encapsulation?
cards.a: 'switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q' before 'switchport mode trunk'. On many modern Catalyst platforms this command is unavailable because 802.1Q is the only supported encapsulation.

cards.q: Does 'switchport nonegotiate' disable 802.1Q?
cards.a: No. It disables DTP negotiation. The port can remain an explicitly configured 802.1Q trunk.

cards.q: What commands verify 802.1Q trunk operation?
cards.a: 'show interfaces trunk' (checks trunk status, encapsulation, native VLAN, allowed VLANs, active VLANs, forwarding/pruning), 'show interfaces Gi0/24 switchport', and 'show vlan brief'.

cards.q: What is the 802.1Q VLAN troubleshooting flow?
cards.a: Check if the link is up, whether it is trunking, whether 802.1Q is operating, whether the VLAN is allowed, whether the VLAN exists, whether STP is forwarding, whether the native VLAN is consistent, and Layer 3 if needed.

cards.q: Is the 802.1Q tag 2 bytes?
cards.a: No. The complete 802.1Q tag is 4 bytes: TPID = 2 bytes plus TCI = 2 bytes.

cards.q: Summarize the 802.1Q quick review key points.
cards.a: IEEE 802.1Q standard for VLAN tagging; tag size 4 bytes; TPID commonly 0x8100; TCI 16 bits; PCP 3-bit L2 priority; DEI 1-bit drop eligible; VID 12 bits; normal VLAN IDs 1-4094; native VLAN normally untagged on trunk; tagged frame adds 4 bytes; typical max tagged frame 1522 bytes; IP MTU commonly stays 1500; modern Cisco trunking is 802.1Q; legacy alternative ISL.

cards.q: What is the one-minute 802.1Q revision chain?
cards.a: 802.1Q = IEEE standard for VLAN tagging; 4-byte tag; TPID + TCI; TCI = PCP + DEI + VID; VID identifies the VLAN; PCP provides Layer 2 priority; native VLAN normally untagged; tagged frame adds 4 bytes; normal VLAN IDs 1-4094; modern Cisco trunking is 802.1Q.
